caption:
A 9-year-old in Castelfidardo, Italy, showed adults a photo of a python poking out of a toilet.
Firefighters and wildlife officers searched for 48 hours before he admitted he made it with an AI app.
He apologized and faces no charges, since children under 14 cannot be held criminally responsible in Italy.

paragraphs.text: A 9-year-old boy in Castelfidardo, a town in the province of Ancona in central Italy, set off a search that lasted 48 hours after showing adults a photo of a python emerging from a toilet, according to the Italian news agency AGI and the entertainment site Dexerto. The snake did not exist. The boy had created the image with an artificial intelligence app.

Dexerto reported that adults raised the alarm at around 8 p.m. on November 12, 2026, after the boy showed them what appeared to be a royal python poking its head out of a toilet bowl. Firefighters from the nearby town of Osimo responded and searched the bathroom and the rest of the property without finding any trace of the animal. According to Dexerto, crews first suspected that the snake had slipped out through an open window or was hiding somewhere inside the home.

The search continued the following day with specialist officers from the Carabinieri Forestali unit that handles protected and exotic species, Dexerto reported. AGI wrote that the alarm was taken at face value for 48 hours and that the town was thrown into turmoil. Some residents believed the python had escaped or gone back down the drain, and coverage on local television news sites and in newspapers added momentum to the hunt, according to AGI.

The truth came out two days after the alarm. According to Dexerto, officers examined the original photo on the boy's phone, and he admitted he had used an AI app to insert the python into a picture of the toilet. AGI reported that he confessed after being pressed by the Carabinieri Forestali, and that he had taken the photo in the bathroom before generating the snake and raising the alarm. Dexerto said he had been visiting a friend at the time.

Dexerto reported that the boy apologized to the officers and will not face legal consequences, because children under the age of 14 cannot be held criminally responsible under Italian law. Neither outlet reported any penalty for the family.

AGI noted that the mayor of Castelfidardo, Roberto Ascani, had recently organized a conference on artificial intelligence in the town. The agency also spoke with Paolo Clini, director of the artificial intelligence department at the Università Politecnica delle Marche, who called it an incredible story and said the subject should be discussed in schools, along with the need not to spread such images so they go viral.

The episode shows how low the barrier to a convincing fake has become. A child with a phone and a consumer app produced an image good enough to send trained firefighters and wildlife specialists on a two-day search, and the deception unraveled only when investigators looked at the original file. The case also shows how quickly local coverage can amplify a false alarm once an image looks real, turning a household scare into a town-wide story before anyone verified the source.

For emergency services, the cost was time and attention spent on a threat that never existed. That cost is small in a case like this one, but the same tools can produce fake evidence of fires, accidents or injured people, where responders cannot afford to wait before acting. Checking the original image on the device that captured it, as the officers eventually did, remains one of the most direct ways to tell a photo from a generated edit.

The calls from Italian academics to teach AI image literacy in schools are likely to grow as cases like this one spread, and the next test is whether schools and emergency services adopt simple routines for checking images before acting on them.
